                                  13            The Court previously dismissed Gafita’s fraud in the inducement claim for a failure
                                  14   to state a claim and insufficiency under the heightened pleading standard of Federal Rule
                                  15   of Civil Procedure 9(b). Order (dkt. 35). Gafita subsequently amended his complaint,
                                  16   splitting his fraud in the inducement claim into two—one for each amendment to his stock
                                  17   purchase agreement. FAC (dkt. 37). Defendants Nucs AI and Nijat Ahmadov move to
                                  18   dismiss these two claims (Gafita’s fifth and sixth claims). Mot. (dkt. 38). As explained
                                  19   below, the Court GRANTS Defendants’ motion in part.1
                                  20   I.       DISCUSSION
                                  21            Gafita alleges that Ahmadov and Farid Yagubbayli (together, “Founder
                                  22   Defendants”) made a series of misstatements that induced him into entering the two
                                  23   amendments that changed the vesting of his initial stock purchase. FAC ¶¶ 104, 114. The
                                  24   Court addresses each claim and its corresponding categories of misstatements below.
                                  25
                                  26
                                       1
                                  27    The Court has already covered the factual allegations and applicable law in its prior order. See
                                       Order. Accordingly, the Court presumes familiarity with the factual and legal backdrop of this
                                  28   motion. The Court also deems this matter suitable for resolution without oral argument, under
                                       Civil Local Rule 7-1(b).
                                         Case 3:25-cv-10757-CRB          Document 43        Filed 08/04/26    Page 2 of 5



                                              A.     First Amendment
                                   1
                                              Gafita alleges that the Founder Defendants made two categories of misstatements
                                   2
                                       for the first amendment: co-founder status and board membership. FAC ¶¶ 104. He
                                   3
                                       asserts that he agreed to revest his shares because, based on the Founder Defendants’
                                   4
                                       statements about his position, he believed he had a key role at Nucs and his equity would
                                   5
                                       be protected. Opp’n (dkt. 40) at 6–9. Defendants’ main argument against these statements
                                   6
                                       is that Gafita fails to allege materiality or reliance as related to the first amendment itself.
                                   7
                                       See Mot. at 15–18. The Court previously dismissed Gafita’s claim based on these
                                   8
                                       categories of statements, partly due to materiality and reliance issues. Order at 13–14
                                   9
                                       (concluding that Gafita’s “complaint does not explain how a promise of a board seat
                                  10
                                       convinced him to later agree to contracts about vesting his shares” (emphasis in original)).
                                  11
                                       For the same reason, the Court dismisses them again.
                                  12
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                              An “inducing representation must not only be material, but must concern an
                                  13
                                       essential part of the transaction.” Maverick Therapeutics, Inc. v. Harpoon Therapeutics,
                                  14
                                       Inc., No. CV 2019-0002-SG, 2020 WL 1655948, at *31 (Del. Ch. Apr. 3, 2020) (citation
                                  15
                                       modified), judgment entered, (Del. Ch. 2020), judgment entered, (Del. Ch. 2021). Gafita
                                  16
                                       still fails to explain how statements about him being a co-founder or getting a board seat
                                  17
                                       concern the essential part of the first amendment: vesting his shares. The Court
                                  18
                                       understands Gafita’s position that the Founder Defendants’ purported scheme lulled him
                                  19
                                       into a false sense of security. See FAC ¶ 28 (representations made Gafita feel “he would
                                  20
                                       be treated fairly”). But statements that are general and unrelated to a contract itself cannot
                                  21
                                       be a basis for a fraud in the inducement claim.
                                  22
                                              Accordingly, the Court dismisses Gafita’s claim as to these statements.
                                  23
                                              B.     Second Amendment
                                  24
                                              Gafita alleges that another two categories of misstatements induced him to agree to
                                  25
                                       the second amendment for his vesting schedule. The first concerns representations that
                                  26
                                       Gafita would be treated fairly and the second is about the necessity of revesting. FAC
                                  27
                                       ¶ 114. Defendants contend that these statements are nonactionable opinions and fail to
                                  28
                                                                                       2
                                         Case 3:25-cv-10757-CRB         Document 43       Filed 08/04/26    Page 3 of 5




                                   1   satisfy Rule 9(b)’s pleading requirements. Mot. at 19–21.
                                   2                 1.     Fairness
                                   3          Gafita points to two statements by Ahmadov that implicate his expected fair
                                   4   treatment. FAC ¶ 114. The first is Ahmadov’s representation that he was a “fair guy” and
                                   5   would treat Gafita fairly. Id. The second is Ahmadov’s statement that Gafita would
                                   6   receive fair compensation for his contributions. Id. Gafita argues that the Court already
                                   7   held that these statements were actionable and that he now adequately alleges them with
                                   8   particularity. Not quite.
                                   9          Gafita’s allegation about Ahmadov being a fair guy who would treat Gafita fairly
                                  10   was not present in the original complaint. And it is not actionable. A “statement of
                                  11   opinion cannot generally be the basis for an action in fraud.” RHA Constr., Inc. v. Scott
                                  12   Eng’g, Inc., No. CVN11C03013JRJCCLD, 2013 WL 3884937, at *4 (Del. Super. Ct. July
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   24, 2013). An opinion can be actionable when there is a “misrepresentation of implied
                                  14   fact.” Id. (internal quotation omitted). Ahmadov’s purported statement is merely an
                                  15   expression of an “opinion[] or prediction[] about the future.” Mooney v. Pioneer Nat. Res.
                                  16   Co., No. CV N17C-01-225 RRC, 2017 WL 4857133, at *5 (Del. Super. Ct. Oct. 24, 2017).
                                  17   There is no underlying fact implicated in his statement. And fairness, after all, is
                                  18   subjective.
                                  19          Ahmadov’s statement about Gafita receiving fair compensation fares differently,
                                  20   however. The Court previously concluded that the statement was actionable because it
                                  21   hinged on Gafita’s compensation and Defendants allegedly schemed to deny Gafita any
                                  22   portion of his shares. Order at 14. The Court only dismissed this misstatement because
                                  23   Gafita failed to provide detailed allegations. Id. at 15. But Gafita properly amended his
                                  24   complaint to add the requisite information. He alleges that the statement was made by
                                  25   Ahmadov around October 2024 at a meeting in Berlin. FAC ¶ 33; see Sultanis v.
                                  26   Champion Petfoods USA Inc., No. 21-CV-00162-EMC, 2021 WL 3373934, at *4 (N.D.
                                  27   Cal. Aug. 3, 2021) (“The circumstances required by Rule 9(b) are the “who, what, when,
                                  28   where, and how” of the activity. (citation modified)).
                                                                                     3
                                         Case 3:25-cv-10757-CRB           Document 43       Filed 08/04/26     Page 4 of 5




                                   1                  2.     Necessity
                                   2          Gafita alleges that Ahmadov made three misstatements about his revesting: (1) his
                                   3   revesting was necessary to secure outside investment; (2) revesting would “be so good for
                                   4   the company”; and (3) Gafita would not “need to work again” after the company
                                   5   succeeded. FAC ¶ 114. Defendants move to dismiss the latter two statements as
                                   6   nonactionable opinions that fail to plead falsity under Rule 9(b). Mot. at 21. The Court
                                   7   agrees that the statements are opinions. Delaware courts are clear that “forward-looking
                                   8   predictions” and puffery are not actionable. Mooney, 2017 WL 4857133, at *5. That is
                                   9   precisely what these statements are. See Trenwick Am. Litig. Tr. v. Ernst & Young,
                                  10   L.L.P., 906 A.2d 168, 208 (Del. Ch. 2006) (non-actionable opinions where the defendant
                                  11   said an acquisition would be “beneficial” or make the company “more competitive in all
                                  12   three of its major markets”), aff’d sub nom. Trenwick Am. Litig. Tr. v. Billett, 931 A.2d
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   438 (Del. 2007). They only refer to a speculative future benefit to Nucs and Gafita.
                                  14   Accordingly, the Court dismisses Gafita’s claim as to these two statements.
                                  15          C.      Fraud by Omission
                                  16          Gafita attempts to salvage his claims by arguing that he is also pursuing a fraud by
                                  17   omission theory under both causes of action. Opp’n at 15. Defendants contend that such a
                                  18   theory is deficient under Rule 9(b). Reply (dkt. 41). The Court agrees with Defendants.
                                  19           Fraud by omission, like affirmative misrepresentations, “must be pleaded with
                                  20   particularity under Rule 9(b).” Kearns v. Ford Motor Co., 567 F.3d 1120, 1127 (9th Cir.
                                  21   2009). To plead an omission with particularity, a plaintiff must “describe the content of
                                  22   the omission and where the omitted information should or could have been revealed” and
                                  23   identify the “representations that plaintiff relied on . . . and that failed to include the
                                  24   allegedly omitted information.” In re NJOY, Inc. Consumer Class Action Litig., No. 14-
                                  25   CV-00428-MMM, 2014 WL 12586074, at *6 (C.D. Cal. Oct. 20, 2014).
                                  26          Gafita’s allegations are plainly deficient. For both claims, Gafita repeats—without
                                  27   detail—that Defendants owed him fiduciary duties to disclose “material facts around their
                                  28   request that he execute” the amendments. See FAC ¶¶ 103, 113. But Gafita fails to plead
                                                                                       4
                                         Case 3:25-cv-10757-CRB        Document 43       Filed 08/04/26   Page 5 of 5




                                   1   what material facts were omitted, merely reiterating that Ahmadov made other
                                   2   affirmatively false misrepresentations. See id. ¶¶ 104, 114.
                                   3   II.    CONCLUSION
                                   4          For the foregoing reasons, the Court GRANTS Defendants’ motion in part. As
                                   5   Gafita already had an opportunity to amend and further amendment would be futile, the
                                   6   Court dismisses with prejudice Gafita’s claims with respect to the misstatements discussed
                                   7   above. Gafita may amend his claims based on his omission theory within 30 days of this
                                   8   order, as amendment may not be futile.
                                   9          IT IS SO ORDERED.
                                  10          Dated: August 4, 2026

14 III.    LEGAL STANDARD
15         The Court may dismiss a complaint for failure to state a claim under Federal Rule of
16 Civil Procedure 12(b)(6) based on either “the lack of a cognizable legal theory or the
17 absence of sufficient facts alleged under a cognizable legal theory.” Godecke v. Kinetic
18 Concepts, Inc., 937 F.3d 1201, 1208 (9th Cir. 2019) (citation modified). A complaint must
19 contain “enough facts to state a claim to relief that is plausible on its face.” Bell Atl. Corp.
20 v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544, 555–56, 570 (2007). A claim is plausible if “the plaintiff pleads
21 factual content that allows the court to draw the reasonable inference that the defendant is
22 liable.” Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662, 678 (2009). “[C]ourts must consider the complaint
23 in its entirety, as well as other sources courts ordinarily examine when ruling on Rule
24 12(b)(6) motions to dismiss, in particular, documents incorporated into the complaint by
25 reference, and matters of which the court may take judicial notice.” Tellabs, Inc. v. Makor
26 Issues & Rights, Ltd., 551 U.S. 308, 322 (2007).
27         In evaluating a fraud-based claim, the Court applies the heightened pleading
28 standard under Rule 9(b). Semegen v. Weidner, 780 F.2d 727, 731 (9th Cir. 1985). Rule
